claims.speaker: Pierre/Peter (hedge fund oil trader, caption spelling varies)
claims.quote: we lost um you know a day of production
claims.claim: Oil stayed at $110 for 3.5 years because about 2 mb/d of supply disruption (Libya, Syria, Iraq, Iran sanctions) offset US shale growth while OPEC covered about 1 mb/d annual demand growth from spare capacity.
claims.indicator: supply disruptions vs US shale growth

claims.speaker: Pierre/Peter (hedge fund oil trader, caption spelling varies)
claims.quote: we had roughly 2 million swing uh in Supply demand balance from June to now and that's why prices came off
claims.claim: From June to autumn 2014 the balance swung by about 2 mb/d (US supply 1.7 vs 1.3 expected, Libya +0.5, demand 0.6 vs 1.3-1.4 expected) and prices fell.

claims.speaker: Pierre/Peter (hedge fund oil trader, caption spelling varies)
claims.quote: we should have at least a two million buyers a day oversupply next year
claims.claim: With US shale up 1.5 mb/d, Libya steady, Iran up and Brazil up, 2015 oversupply is at least 2 mb/d, which cannot persist because storage fills within six months, so prices must adjust.

claims.speaker: Pierre/Peter (hedge fund oil trader, caption spelling varies)
claims.quote: they would just shoot themselves in the food by keep on cutting production
claims.claim: OPEC alone cutting 2 mb/d each year would lose share to US shale and not stop price falls; stabilising needs slower US growth or new disruptions.

claims.speaker: Pierre/Peter (hedge fund oil trader, caption spelling varies)
claims.quote: when I look at you know marginal cost of production of shaylord and I look at what people were saying in natural gas in 2008
claims.claim: Marginal cost falls with technology: natural gas was said to need $7 in 2008 and now $3, so shale oil's marginal cost will also fall, implying a bear market.

claims.speaker: Pierre/Peter (hedge fund oil trader, caption spelling varies)
claims.quote: there's not no like stable oil price that can last for the next 10 years
claims.claim: The three-year stability was by chance (masking disruptions); expect cycles of lower and higher prices, lower first, then lower prices cut supply growth and revive demand, planting the next rally.

claims.speaker: Pierre/Peter (hedge fund oil trader, caption spelling varies)
claims.quote: demand is so inelastic if we basically um ten percent move in the price it has an impact of maybe 0.15 percent
claims.claim: Short-run oil demand is very inelastic: a 10% price move shifts demand about 0.15%, so price must move a lot to rebalance.

claims.speaker: Pierre/Peter (hedge fund oil trader, caption spelling varies)
claims.quote: so far we haven't had Supply disruption from Iraq despite what's going on with Isis
claims.claim: Supply disruptions that had propped up the 2011-14 price are fading: Libya returned unexpectedly, Iran sanctions eased, Iraq (despite ISIS) and Russia (despite Ukraine) have not lost output, and the Russia sanctions may have hit European demand rather than supply, so geopolitical headlines did not tighten supply in 2014.
claims.indicator: Libyan, Iranian, Iraqi and Russian crude output; supply disruption total
claims.direction: bearish oil as disruption premium fades
claims.conditions: when geopolitical events do not actually remove barrels
claims.testable: yes - compare disruption volumes with price changes

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: I have one analyst who very good and who in January Pi you should look at CoCo
claims.claim: Andurand, mainly an energy and metals trader, entered cocoa because an analyst proposed it, and then both dug deep into fundamentals to build a thesis outside his usual markets.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: most analysts out there have it down 11% but that's because they tend to be very conservative you know they have lot of clients and they don't want to worry the world
claims.claim: Andurand sees cocoa production down about 17.7% versus the consensus of 11% because sell-side analysts give conservative estimates to avoid alarming clients, so consensus lags a supply shock.
claims.conditions: when own tracking of exports diverges from consensus

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: really tracking the export from the the main exporters mainly Ivory Coast and Ghana that wees together about 60% of world's production
claims.claim: Tracking exports of Ivory Coast and Ghana (about 60% of world supply) showed shipments down 30% and 41% year to date, a direct high-frequency read on the supply deficit.
claims.indicator: Ivory Coast and Ghana cocoa port exports

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: that represent only 20% of the balance of the season for West Africa and and that's not going to be enough to to really change the deficit that we have this year
claims.claim: The mid-crop represents only about 20% of the rest of the season so it cannot close the roughly 800,000 ton deficit (about 5 million ton market).

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: at first you eat into current inventories until you run out of inventories and then the price can go anywhere
claims.claim: A supply deficit is first absorbed by drawing inventories, and once inventories run out price has no ceiling and must rise until demand is destroyed.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: demand is extremely inelastic I mean you can study that historically when you have a recession or not when prices go up a lot or not I mean demand generally goes up
claims.claim: Cocoa demand is extremely inelastic historically, so the price was capped at $2,500-3,000 by supply, not demand, and a supply shortfall must be cleared by price alone.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: people consume 1.7 grams of cocoa per day which at $110,000 a ton represents 1.7 Cent per day
claims.claim: Back-of-envelope: 5 million tons of demand over 8 billion people means a few cents per person per day even at very high cocoa prices, so higher prices barely hit consumers' budgets and do not cut consumption.
claims.indicator: cocoa cost as share of consumer spending
claims.conditions: cocoa content in chocolate small (milk chocolate under 10%)
claims.testable: yes - arithmetic on demand and price

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: 70% in West Africa and then you have a 21% in main Latin America and 5% in Asia and Oceania
claims.claim: Cocoa production is concentrated near a latitude band needing specific temperature, rainfall and humidity: 70% West Africa, 21% Latin America, 5% Asia and Oceania, so local shocks hit global supply.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: some of it due to El Nino we had um basically period of time when when it was too hot and period of time when we had way way too much rain
claims.claim: El Nino caused heat and excess rain that cut the cocoa crop, and La Nina next year should help at the margin, making part of the shortfall cyclical.
claims.conditions: El Nino hurts West African cocoa, La Nina helps

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: climate change is every year Shifting the weather patterns generally unfavorably for Coco Productions
claims.claim: Climate change steadily shifts weather patterns unfavorably for cocoa, a structural drag on supply that does not reverse with a good season.
claims.testable: partly - hard to separate from cycle

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: a tree that has that swollen Sho disease loses 25% yield within the first last year and 50% within two years and the tree dies within 3 to four years
claims.claim: Swollen shoot virus (known since 1936, spread by mealybugs) cuts yield 25% in a year and 50% in two and kills trees in 3 to 4 years; its spread over the last year is a structural supply loss.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: black pot disease that that come from a fungus and it occurs mainly during the rainy season it's spread by by rain splash
claims.claim: Black pod fungus spreads by rain splash in wet seasons, so heavy rain such as in El Nino years raises disease losses.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: less usage of fertilizers mainly in Ivory Coast due to high fertilizer prices and and also shortages due to the Russian invasion of Ukraine
claims.claim: Ivory Coast farmers used less fertilizer due to high prices and Russia-Ukraine shortages, cutting yields; it will not reverse soon because farmers still receive low prices.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: the farmers are still getting relatively low prices and they're still struggling to make and meat
claims.claim: Farmer-gate prices stayed low, so farmers cannot afford inputs and no supply response from fertilizer is expected: Andurand sees the supply problems as largely structural rather than weather.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: you have some Consultants that are specialized and every month they have a team doing surveys of the main produc regions
claims.claim: Even in a less transparent market, specialist consultants survey the main producing regions monthly, giving enough data to forecast next year's crop.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: they believe okay the top of the range is a high price for Apple but they don't really ask themselves what makes that price right
claims.claim: Experienced traders anchor on the historical price range and do not ask what price is needed to balance the market; stepping back to compute the balancing price gives an edge.
claims.conditions: after structural change in supply response

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: would have the supply response if prices were going up but if now you get you don't get the supply response or the supply response takes four or five years then you need to have a demand response
claims.claim: If a price rise no longer triggers a quick supply response (cocoa trees take 4-5 years), the market can clear only through demand, requiring a much larger price rise.
claims.direction: long when supply response is delayed
claims.testable: partly - lag between price and supply

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: previous High in 1977 was 5,500 something doll a ton of $1 1977 which is equivalent to $28,000 a ton of today's dollar
claims.claim: Judged in real terms, the 1977 cocoa peak equals about $28,000 a ton today, so the nominal 'all-time high' headline overstates how stretched prices are.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: you have to like look at a bit more history and and understand in the past how prices reacted to a shortage how long it took to recover
claims.claim: Use historical shortages to see how prices reacted and how long supply took to recover, then adjust for what is different today.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: there's a ratio that we look at that most people look at it's actually the inventory to to grinding ratio so it's it's a measure of inventory to demand
claims.claim: The key balance indicator is the stocks-to-grindings ratio (inventory divided by industrial processing demand).

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: grindings look to be down three three and a half% this year despite the fact that the end demand is the same in volume
claims.claim: Grindings fell 3-3.5% while chocolate demand was flat in volume, meaning destocking at every level of the chain (beans, butter, powder), which hides how short the market is.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: now we have the largest deficit ever on top of two previous years of deficit and it looks like next year we will have a deficit
claims.claim: A record deficit after two earlier deficit years, and another expected, puts the stocks-to-grindings ratio around 21% versus 35-40% in the last decade.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: at 19% and that's what drove us to $28,000 a ton of today's dollars
claims.claim: In 1977 a 19% stocks-to-grindings ratio drove cocoa to about $28,000 in today's dollars, the historical analogue for the current 21%.
claims.direction: long cocoa at very low ratio

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: if we have another deficit next year then we we might go down to 13%
claims.claim: Another deficit year would push the ratio to about 13%, an outright shortage of beans where price must explode since demand cannot be slowed.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: if you have no physical somebody wants to take delivery the price can go anywhere so it's a dangerous commodity to short
claims.claim: Physically settled futures converge to the physical price, so with no physical available shorts face unbounded squeezes.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: the fonts have been selling since February they actually went from a a length of 175,000 Lots
claims.claim: Funds (speculators) cut longs by more than 80% from 175,000 lots to 28,000 since February, so the cocoa rally was not fund-driven; claims that funds pushed prices were untrue.
claims.indicator: speculative fund net long in cocoa futures (COT)

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: the people who've been buying futures from the fonts it's producers because they're producing a lot less than
claims.claim: Producers who had sold forward were buying back futures from funds because their crops fell short of expectations, a source of buying not seen in positioning headlines.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: and then we get into a market where you have less liquidity because you have less exposure you have less Longs and less less shorts and then the Vol volatility increases
claims.claim: As the price moved massively, open interest shrank, liquidity thinned and volatility rose, causing traders to cut position sizes, which in turn makes prices even more volatile.
claims.testable: yes - open interest and vol data

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: you have to calibrate your position to to be able to take a 50% move Mo against you on the way
claims.claim: In an illiquid, volatile commodity size so that a 50% adverse move can be survived; being right on direction is not enough.
claims.conditions: illiquid market with large deficit and low inventories

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: you have to be out completely because I still think that there's more upside than downside I think we still have the potential to go above $20,000 a ton later this year
claims.claim: Andurand stayed long cocoa with about $2,000 downside (December contract $7,000 to $5,000) versus $13-15k upside (over $20,000), a skewed payoff.
claims.testable: no - single view, time-bound to May 2024

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: for that you need a lot of things need to go right you need like a bumper crop in West Africa next year
claims.claim: The bearish scenario needs a bumper West African crop and near-perfect weather for the rest of the year, so the probability of a drop is not zero but low.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: if we have the production going back up roughly 10% from this year to next year we still have a deficit of 300,000 tons or so next year
claims.claim: Even a 10% production rebound leaves a deficit of about 300,000 tons next year, bringing the ratio to about 13%, far below 1977.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: then the prices will probably come off from here towards you know I don't know five or $6,000 a ton
claims.claim: If surveys over the next four months show a great Ivory Coast and Ghana crop, the price should fall toward $5-6k but not back to $2,500.
claims.indicator: crop surveys of Ivory Coast and Ghana
claims.direction: exit cocoa on strong crop surveys
claims.testable: partly - surveys are a leading indicator

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: because we need we have a very low inventory so we need to rebuild stocks everywhere
claims.claim: Because inventories are very low, prices cannot drop back to old levels; stocks must be rebuilt across the supply chain, which keeps a demand floor.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: in Europe only 20% of the the inventories on Exchange 20% of the European stocks are on Exchange the others are really with with the chocolate makers
claims.claim: Cocoa inventory data are partial: US stocks are on exchange but only 20% of European stocks are; port stocks in Ivory Coast and Ghana are visible, and specialist firms estimate the rest with cross-validation.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: you have this underlying climate change that is also a trend that really impact production over time
claims.claim: Beyond random weather, climate change creates a trending structural impact on soft commodity production that offers theme opportunities beyond cocoa.
claims.testable: partly - hard to separate from weather

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: three to five years for that Cocoa Tree to give you cocoa beans
claims.claim: Tree crops take 3-5 years to respond to price versus immediate replanting for grains, so supply response is slow.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: so it should makees make it easier in a way to have position that you can hold for longer that are a bit more structural than than for GRS
claims.claim: Because supply responds slowly, shocks create larger and longer moves in cocoa than in grains, making it easier to hold structural positions.
claims.conditions: tree crops with slow supply response

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: versus Coco where you have many one Mega major producer and another very large one
claims.claim: Cocoa is easier to analyze than grains because production is concentrated in one mega producer and one large producer, so a few data points give a good read on next year's crop.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: demand was growing about half a million ton a year and Supply was growing half a million ton a year in average
claims.claim: For 15-20 years copper was balanced, with demand and supply each growing about 0.5 million tons a year.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: Renewables take a lot more copper than like nuclear plants or like fossil fuel generated electricity
claims.claim: Electrification of transport, grid expansion for renewables (solar, wind) and data centers add new copper demand, much copper-intensive versus nuclear or fossil power.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: we see Market in which we are going to have overall 1 million tons of demand per year roughly of demand increase per year and the supply growth basically by the end of next year will be zero to negative
claims.claim: Despite weaker Chinese property demand, copper demand grows about 1 million tons a year while mine supply growth goes to zero or negative within 12-18 months, producing a widening multi-year deficit.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: a bunch of like pods that have very many many teams in in those big multi strategy funds that have very tight draw Downs so they tend to try to trade for the next few days
claims.claim: Copper has not priced the coming deficit because most hedge fund capital sits in multi-strategy pods with tight drawdown limits that cannot hold positions beyond days or weeks, so the market gives no early price signal to fix a multi-year deficit.
claims.direction: long-horizon investors can earn the deficit premium
claims.testable: partly - structural claim about market participants

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: if you bring a new mine it's like more than 10 years to bring it's like 10 to 15 years to bring a new mine
claims.claim: New copper mines take 10-15 years and growth is shifting to less stable countries, so supply cannot respond quickly to price.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: the price of copper is a very small percentage of the price of the end product right so if copper goes up 10 times I mean your end product will go up a little bit
claims.claim: Copper demand is inelastic because copper is a small fraction of end-product cost and the energy transition must proceed regardless of price, so the price move needed to balance the market is large.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: we look at it year year by year so so we think okay at current prices what would be the supply and demand balance
claims.claim: Method for a fair price: model supply and demand year by year at current prices, assess price sensitivity of each side, and treat the price path (not a single price) as the question.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: when prices go up you get more scrap Supply that that comes as a source of supply for copper
claims.claim: Scrap supply is the only quick supply response to higher copper prices, while mine supply does not respond for years; demand shifting to later is limited.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: we're going to get about like 400 to 500,000 tons deficit and we had less than that in terms of visible stocks at the beginning of the year
claims.claim: Projected 2024 deficit of 400-500k tons exceeds visible stocks, so visible inventories could run out by year-end.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: if they know that we're going to at the beginning of a multi-year deficit they're not going to sell their strategic reserves in the first year
claims.claim: China's strategic reserve (SRB) is an extra inventory but would not be sold early in a multi-year deficit, so it cannot cap prices.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: deficit that are more than a million tons and eventually more than 3 million tons in 2030
claims.claim: Deficits accumulate to more than 1 million tons in 2026 and over 3 million tons by 2030, exceeding inventory buffers.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: we're going to have to have a non nonlinear move sooner than later because of the large deficit
claims.claim: With a large deficit, low inventories and inelastic demand, copper must move non-linearly to force demand destruction, possibly a multiple of the price rather than 20%.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: I think they could go up four times so know over 5 year 5 year Horizon
claims.claim: Andurand sees copper potentially quadrupling over a five-year horizon, since a 20% move would not change the supply-demand balance.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: we all expecting to see at least some decline in Russian production due to sanctions or due to issues in Russia and and at the end we there was no no Supply response at all
claims.claim: Expected oil supply disruptions in 2022-23 (Russia sanctions, Iran) did not materialize: Russian output held, Iranian exports surged on weak enforcement and US supply grew faster than expected, so consensus overestimated disruption.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: I mean is US shell production about to Peak or not we don't know we'll only know it after the fact
claims.claim: US shale growth has disappointed over the last four months, which may be the start of a peak but four months is not yet a trend.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: if the conflict stays between Israel and Gaza I mean there's no oil there it has no impact at all on o o oil supply
claims.claim: Real supply loss would need an attack on Iranian oil facilities, prompting Iran to hit Saudi facilities or close Hormuz, which is low probability; the Gaza conflict alone has no oil supply impact.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: the ukrainians have not attacked pipelines and ports yet I think if they really wanted to to impact the revenues of Russia they should attack the ports
claims.claim: Ukrainian strikes have hit Russian refineries not ports or crude pipelines, which would be the way to cut Russian revenue and would impact supply.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: the Biden Administration is very very paranoid about having high gasoline prices before the election
claims.claim: The US pressures Ukraine not to hit Russian ports before the election to avoid high gasoline prices, but a more desperate Ukraine might attack them, creating a supply-disruption risk.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: it's just a question of geology and and money actually more than anything
claims.claim: US oil supply growth is set by geology and capital rather than who is president, and US output is probably near peak, so the election matters marginally for production.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: I would expect Trump to enforce the sanctions on Iran more tightly so we might lose some oil from Iran
claims.claim: A Trump presidency would probably enforce Iran sanctions more tightly, removing some Iranian oil, partly offset by more Saudi supply, so overall effect on oil prices is small.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: the price can go up 10 times your your tablet is only going to double in price
claims.claim: Pass-through is muted because milk chocolate contains under 10% cocoa: a tenfold rise in cocoa roughly doubles a bar's price, and even a heavy high-cocoa chocolate eater pays only about $10 a month more (a moderate eater $2 to $5), so higher cocoa prices do not reduce consumption.
claims.indicator: cocoa share of chocolate retail price and consumer budget
claims.conditions: demand-side inelasticity at the consumer level

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: the prices of both those elements also went up even more than cocoa beans which means that actually we probably had some destocking
claims.claim: Cocoa butter and powder prices rose even more than beans, which Andurand reads as evidence of destocking at the processing level as well, consistent with demand being met from inventories along the chain rather than from new production.
claims.indicator: cocoa butter and powder prices relative to beans
claims.testable: partly - product price ratios are observable

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: we looked at cofi quickly it it looked less uh it looked interesting as well because you get big losses in production from Vietnam
claims.claim: Andurand screened coffee (large Vietnamese production losses) and judged it interesting but not exciting enough to trade, and had not looked at orange juice, showing he picks only supply shocks big enough to dominate the balance.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: it's a market that's driven by geopolitical events there's been a lot of reading trying to understand you know how the war will pan out
claims.claim: In a geopolitically driven market, the work is reading how the war and sanctions will evolve, and calls are hard to make with confidence.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: already with very low inventories with the low speed capacity in the hands of opec and in general low production capacity spare production capacity a low expected supply growth and high expected demand goals
claims.claim: Before the invasion, oil already had very low inventories, little OPEC spare capacity, low expected supply growth and strong post-Covid demand, so fundamentals were very strong independent of Russia.
claims.testable: yes - inventory and spare capacity data

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: backwardation means the front end the first contracts are much higher than the back contracts and and it means that the market is very tight physically
claims.claim: Backwardation (front contracts above deferred) measures physical tightness; Brent backwardation was about $2 a month before the invasion and $4-5 after, with gasoil above $50 a barrel between two months.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: there haven't been like massive disruptions yet it's just the fears of how the sanctions will bite that that keeps the market tight
claims.claim: Prices were already high on fear of sanctions before actual supply loss, so the move could be the beginning or the end, which makes strong calls difficult.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: study the fundamentals of the market studies the growth of demand relative to the growth of supply and as a result uh you know have an idea if inventories are going to go up on or down
claims.claim: Process: model demand growth versus supply growth to project inventory direction and the price needed to balance the market so storage or inventory limits are not breached.
claims.direction: long when inventories fall, short when they build

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: so for me i'm trying to make money from the large moves in the old market
claims.claim: Andurand is directionally agnostic: he has been short (late 2008, 2014-15, before Covid) and long, seeking the large oil moves that last months to years.
claims.direction: long or short large oil trends

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: we don't sell options we either flat options or long options
claims.claim: Andurand never sells options; he is flat or long calls and puts, so risk is capped at premium.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: when when we feel like the market is going to you know make a big move in a short period of time then we prefer to be to express that view with options relative to futures
claims.claim: When expecting a big move in a short period he expresses the view with long options rather than futures, getting more leverage with less risk.
claims.testable: partly - option vs futures payoff testable

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: it's really important to understand the physical because it's what's going to drive the price of oil
claims.claim: Understanding physical inventories, storage and delivery mechanics is essential even for a futures-only trader because physical balance drives price.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: the level of uh empty storage was um enough was actually could only take one and a half months of this really low demand before all the tanks were full
claims.claim: In April 2020 demand fell 20% overnight and empty storage could absorb only about 1.5 months of surplus, after which unstorable oil drove prices negative.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: if somebody is long futures and try to take delivery of of oil at that at that place and that point in time well nobody can deliver and then you can go to any price
claims.claim: The mirror case: with empty tanks at delivery points such as Cushing, a long who stands for delivery cannot be filled and price can spike without limit.
claims.direction: long oil when delivery stocks are depleted

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: the price should move in order to keep the the inventories within kind of uh kind of in range that makes the market function
claims.claim: The role of speculators is price discovery: prices must move enough to keep inventories between empty and full, and if they lag prices later have to overshoot.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: now u.s shell has been producing you know at scale for 10 years and there's still room you know for another you know 10 years of also of strong supply
claims.claim: US shale has already drilled much of the easy oil and fields are maturing, so about 10 more years of strong supply is possible but not decades of high growth.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: the whole industry had burned through 600 billion dollars of cash and the shareholders had taken a big hit
claims.claim: US shale producers burned about $600 billion of cash while growing production, so shareholders lost heavily.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: the shareholders of those companies pressure the the ceos to not grow production too fast because if they grow it too fast then prices crash again
claims.claim: Now profitable, shale producers face shareholder and climate pressure to keep capital discipline, which limits the supply response to high prices.
claims.direction: higher prices needed, supply response muted

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: there hasn't been a lot of work in giving a solution for the consumers right to have another choice but to buy oil
claims.claim: Pressure on oil supply to fall has outrun alternatives for consumers, so oil demand cannot shift quickly and shortages result.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: there's not enough power to charge those evs so we will have an issue at least in europe in finding a solution for for power supply
claims.claim: Replacing combustion cars with EVs is limited by grid power supply, especially in Europe, which slows decarbonization of oil demand.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: the growth of supply in metals is not going to be large enough to build as many evs and to electrify the world as fast as we'd like because the miners have not invested enough
claims.claim: Metal supply is too small for fast electrification because miners underinvested under ESG pressure, and renewables, batteries and EVs are copper-intensive.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: metals prices will have to go up a lot in order to incentivize enough supply growth to be able to decarbonize the world
claims.claim: Decarbonization needs much higher metals prices to induce the supply growth required.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: they will not do it before they understand that the russian oil is out and will not come back in time soon
claims.claim: Gulf producers (Saudi, Kuwait) and the US could add about 1.5 mb/d but only after Russian supply is visibly gone, not preemptively, against a potential 4 mb/d loss.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: i still think that the sanctions will stay on russia until the west can feel like they can trust them
claims.claim: Sanctions would stay until the West trusts Russia again, which Andurand thinks requires regime change, so Russian oil would not return quickly even after a ceasefire.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: even though we don't have formal sanctions yet from the eu in practice not everybody can buy oil
claims.claim: Self-sanctioning by refiners, insurers and banks (no insurance for ships, no letters of credit even from Chinese banks) restricts Russian oil sales before formal sanctions.
claims.indicator: Russian oil sales, insurance and letters of credit
claims.testable: partly - discount of Urals to Brent

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: russia will have to stop production because they will run out of storage capacity at their ports and and and so basically they will need to cut production by two at least two million bars a day
claims.claim: If Russian cargoes cannot be sold, port storage fills within weeks and Russia must shut in 2-3 mb/d, which takes time to restore.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: making europe is very dependent on russian gas gas has been natural gas mainly germany and italy
claims.claim: Europe, especially Germany and Italy, depends on Russian gas and may ration demand and accelerate the energy transition, which in turn needs metals.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: they could release up to 5 million barrels a day for 12 months
claims.claim: Strategic petroleum reserves of IEA members can release up to 5 mb/d for 12 months (about 2 mb/d for 2.5 years) but leave reserves empty and need refilling.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: or it will have to be coming from price and then the price will have to be high enough to bring that demand down by one and a half million bucks a day also
claims.claim: After SPR and Gulf supply, about 1.5 mb/d (roughly 2%) of demand must be destroyed through government mandates or price.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: you don't really generally have such thing as demand destruction for oil because you can't really replace in the short term right
claims.claim: Short-run oil demand is inelastic because consumers cannot replace cars quickly, so demand destruction comes from economic crises, not price alone.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: maybe they'll use their cars a bit less for one or two months and then they'll get used to the new price
claims.claim: A price spike only slows driving for one or two months before consumers adapt, so it is not real demand destruction.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: what brings demand down that's when we have large recessions so not small recessions but large recessions
claims.claim: Oil prices fall when large recessions cut demand, not small ones, so the price level at which demand falls depends on the economic environment.
claims.testable: yes - oil demand vs recession size

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: at the time we didn't see that demand was being hit but when le mans went burst
claims.claim: In 2008 oil reached $147 (about $200 today) without hurting demand until Lehman failed and the credit and trade-finance collapse crushed demand.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: and the economy could you know handle 150 dollars of today's dollars for for three and a half years
claims.claim: Brent averaged $110 (about $150 today) from 2011 to mid-2014 despite the euro crisis, showing the economy tolerates high real oil prices for years.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: i was expecting already prices to go above 150 before the russian invasion
claims.claim: Andurand expected oil above $150 before the invasion; the move was accelerated, not caused, by Russia.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: that the market doesn't believe that um we will lose this oil for very long
claims.claim: Brent at only $114 implies the market assumes the Russian outage is short, which is a mispricing relative to Andurand's view.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: then i think that uh around 200 oil will be enough to to bring demand down to balance the market
claims.claim: Absent mandates, oil around $200 would be needed to bring demand into balance; there is no demand destruction at $110, and 200 is possible within the year.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: they collectively you know agreed to cut production by around 10 million barrels a day
claims.claim: OPEC+ cut 10 mb/d in April 2020 and stayed compliant for over a year, restoring supply only gradually, which prevented a larger collapse.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: quite a few countries in opec plus could not meet dakota many of the african countries they could not produce as much as what they were allowed to because of under investment
claims.claim: Many OPEC+ members, especially African ones, cannot fill quotas because of underinvestment, so quota increases do not translate into barrels.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: i think it's probably uh only saudi kuwait and uae and that's pretty much it
claims.claim: Real spare production capacity (sustainable for 1-2 years) is only about 1.5 mb/d and sits with Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and the UAE.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: that will take you know 12 months also for for the u.s to be able to bring higher levels of supply than what is expected today
claims.claim: A US supply response above current expectations needs about 12 months, so near-term balances stay tight.
claims.testable: yes - rig count to output lag

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: i think basically if a country had a currency backed to gold or something well the western world could still sanction that currency even if it's backed by gold
claims.claim: Gold-backed or crypto-based currency does not protect against sanctions because reserves can be frozen, so the dollar's reserve status is not easily displaced.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: currencies in general it's always going to be countries that have a strong rule of law and and trust and a strong financial market that will be able to have a strong currency
claims.claim: Strong currencies need rule of law, low corruption, freedom and deep financial markets, which China lacks as it holds large US Treasuries and capital controls.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: what we need is to be able to eat and move so it's energy it's energy it's agricultural products it's food it's metal
claims.claim: To protect against high inflation, hold real needs (energy, agricultural products, metals) rather than crypto.
claims.testable: yes - commodity returns in inflation regimes

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: most of the pension funds don't have a box saying we have to be long commodities
claims.claim: Pension funds have no commodity allocation, so as commodities become important more investment flow should come, funding supply.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: for agricultural products it's pretty fast like within a year you can change things but for metals it takes anywhere between seven and fifteen years
claims.claim: Supply response time differs: agriculture within a year, metals 7-15 years, and new oil projects about 7 years, so long-lead supply cannot fix near-term shortages.
claims.direction: long metals and oil in shortage

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: for any any new projects generally today would bring oil uh supply in seven years time
claims.claim: New non-shale oil projects take about 7 years, and hesitation about demand in 2029-30 discourages long-lead investment.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: only the u.s has a shorter cycle of probably 12 months before the decision to increase capex and getting more oil
claims.claim: Only US shale responds within about a year to higher prices, so supply additions come from the US first and the rest later.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: over the next 10 years commodities are gonna cap the community's supply actually not only price but level of supply will actually cap the type of economic growth we will be able to have
claims.claim: Over the next decade commodity supply, not just price, will constrain economic growth; economic models that assume unlimited commodity supply are wrong.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: once we get less supply of any other commodities and also very low unemployment number you know it's hard to find the people
claims.claim: Bottlenecks in other commodities (steel, sand), labour shortages and low unemployment hinder new oil supply, so tight markets reinforce each other.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: this time we might not have it
claims.claim: Unlike 2008-2011, when shale then helped, there may be no equivalent supply response now, so the current setup is more bullish than 2008.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: so 150 dollars then is 220 today in today's dollars
claims.claim: In global GDP deflator terms $150 in 2008 equals about $220 today, so record nominal prices understate real stretch.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: they get used to higher levels over time
claims.claim: Consumers complain at $100, $120, $140 but adapt, so demand adjusts only slowly through marginal usage like shorter trips; recency bias makes prices look too high.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: today for one unit of gdp we're used we are using 15 less oil than in in 2008
claims.claim: Oil use per unit of GDP is 15% lower than in 2008, so the economic impact of $150 in 2008 is closer to that of about $250 today.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: i think it's a new territory i can't speak of an event that was similar over the last few decades really
claims.claim: The combined shock (very tight inventories, war, sanctions and self-sanctions) has no close precedent in recent decades, so historical analogues give little guidance on how far prices can move.
claims.conditions: Applies to the March 2022 war-driven supply shock; analogue-based sizing is unreliable.
claims.testable: no - a judgement about regime novelty, not a measurable signal

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: sometimes we'll bet that prices will go up for sometimes for a few months or a few years and and sometimes we'll bet that they go down over generally a few months
claims.claim: Andurand holds bullish oil positions for months to years but bearish positions generally for a few months up to about a year, an asymmetry in the holding period of his large-move trades.
claims.direction: long oil trades run longer than short oil trades
claims.conditions: Both directions are traded; holding period is set by the size of the supply-demand imbalance.
claims.testable: partly - durations could be checked against historical oil trend lengths

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: and we'll pick like a month for example if we want to be long the front month contract
claims.claim: Bullish views are expressed through Brent, WTI, heating oil or gasoline futures with a chosen contract month: the front month for a near-term tightness view, or a deferred month (for example December Brent) for a view further along the curve.
claims.indicator: Brent / WTI / heating oil / RBOB futures, choice of contract month on the curve
claims.direction: long front month or long deferred month
claims.conditions: Choice of curve point reflects where the view on tightness sits in time.
claims.testable: yes - curve-point choice (front versus deferred) can be backtested against roll and spread returns

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: the shareholders of those companies pressure the the ceos to not grow production too fast because if they grow it too fast then prices crash again and then they can be losing money
claims.claim: The shale supply response is self-limiting because producers know that rapid output growth would crash prices again and destroy profits, so shareholders push managers to hold output growth back even when prices are high.
claims.indicator: US shale capex and production growth versus oil price
claims.direction: slower US supply growth, price stays higher for longer
claims.conditions: Holds while the industry's memory of the cash burn (about $600 billion) persists and investors demand returns.
claims.testable: partly - shale capex discipline and rig counts versus price could be tested

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: it takes time to build solar panels and windmills and to build enough evs and enough charging stations and all that
claims.claim: The decarbonization build-out (renewables, EVs, charging) is a roughly 20-year transition that cannot replace lost fossil supply overnight, so a sudden loss of Russian oil must be met by other fossil supply or by lower demand; the system is already at capacity in the short term.
claims.direction: oil stays needed in the near term, no fast substitution
claims.conditions: Short-run only; the long-run transition plan is unchanged.
claims.testable: no - qualitative statement on substitution speed

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: if there's a region change in one week i mean i think it's unlikely but you never know
claims.claim: The sanctions scenario is conditional on regime change: if a trusted government emerged quickly, Russian oil could return in a few months, but without it the supply stays out even after fighting stops, so the duration of the outage is the key swing factor for the oil price.
claims.indicator: Russian oil export availability, sanctions status
claims.direction: Russian supply returns in months only with regime change and normal relations
claims.conditions: He judges the quick regime change scenario unlikely.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: russia is a big exporter of metals so it's not it's not going to be easy
claims.claim: Accelerating the European energy transition to cut Russian gas use needs more metals, but Russia is a big metals exporter, so the sanctions shock tightens the very supply the substitution depends on.
claims.indicator: Russian metals exports, energy transition metals demand
claims.conditions: Compounds the existing metals underinvestment problem.
claims.testable: partly - metals price response to Russian supply loss could be checked

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: here if we just need to to think of bringing all demand down by two percent it's not going to be as drastic as a global lockdown
claims.claim: Demand destruction can come from government mandates rather than price: the Covid lockdown cut oil demand about 20%, whereas the shortfall now needs only about 2%, so mandates such as a few confinement days a month could close the gap without a recession.
claims.indicator: oil demand cut required (about 2% of global demand)
claims.conditions: Only if governments choose mandates; otherwise the price must rise to near $200 to clear the market.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: we'll probably get to deal with iran bringing a million buyers a day back but that's expected by the market
claims.claim: A return of about 1 mb/d of Iranian supply is likely but already expected by the market, so it does not offset the Russian shortfall that the price still has to reflect; only unexpected supply moves prices.
claims.direction: Iran supply is priced in, no extra bearish effect
claims.conditions: Assumes a nuclear deal and sanctions relief on Iran.
claims.testable: partly - priced-in versus surprise supply could be tested around announcements

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: it's going to be at least five years before the decision when a company decides to bring the production of certain metals or minerals up and when that supply will come
claims.claim: Metals and minerals supply cannot respond for at least five years after a production decision; permitting will probably be faster at much higher prices, but there is no short-term fix for next year or two years out.
claims.indicator: metals and minerals supply lead times
claims.direction: metals prices stay high until new supply arrives
claims.conditions: Lead time shortens somewhat when prices are very high and approvals speed up.
claims.testable: partly - lead times can be measured from project data

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: i think we'll have to live with higher prices to keep you know demand down uh to keep um to to be treated a bit more as a luxury product and also to accelerate the energy transition
claims.claim: Because supply cannot respond quickly, oil prices have to stay high enough for a prolonged period to keep demand down, treating oil as a luxury product and pushing the energy transition forward.
claims.indicator: oil price level over the next few years
claims.conditions: Until non-US supply and alternatives arrive.
claims.testable: no - view on the price path

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: only the u.s has a shorter cycle of probably 12 months before the decision to increase capex and getting more oil because they know where they only have all the infrastructure
claims.claim: US shale responds fastest, about 12 months from capex decision to oil, because the wells, infrastructure and service-company capacity already exist; other supply regions lack these so respond later.
claims.indicator: US shale infrastructure and oilfield-services capacity
claims.direction: US supply is the first to rise
claims.conditions: Needs spare service capacity; bottlenecks in labour, steel and sand can slow it.
claims.testable: partly - rig counts and services capacity versus price lag could be tested

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: once politicians understand that we have to plan for no Russian gas then it is much easier than you know assuming that it will come and then it doesn't
claims.claim: Planning for zero Russian gas (exports to Europe already down 75%) makes the adjustment feasible and avoids the worst case of assuming supply that does not arrive.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: pretty much almost double the the Imports of LNG and that increasing LNG Supply corresponds to about two cells of the Russian losses so far
claims.claim: Europe nearly doubled LNG imports, covering about two thirds of lost Russian gas, and new import capacity is coming, so import capacity is not the constraint.
claims.direction: less upside risk in European gas

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: Europe being you know what you know like one of the wealthiest continents that they'll be able to most of the competitors for for LNG
claims.claim: Europe's wealth lets it outbid other LNG buyers, so the physical shortage is pushed onto poorer importers.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: if we assume that Europe could attract about 40 percent of the LNG additions that will already go a long way in solving solving the crisis
claims.claim: If Europe captures about 40% of global LNG additions (a big bump in 2025) it can replace much of the Russian gas, though not all within two years, so a demand response is needed.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: about 50 is coming from residential slash commercial demand that for heating and cooking but mainly Heating about uh 25 is coming from industrial demand twenty percent of Southern power
claims.claim: Gas demand split is about 50% residential/commercial (mostly heating), 25% industrial and 20% power, which shows where cuts can be made.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: so far we've seen a switch of about 35 percent for oil in the industrial demand
claims.claim: High gas relative to oil prices already shifted about 35% of industrial gas demand to oil, so gas demand destruction began before winter.
claims.conditions: gas much more expensive than oil

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: we need to bring the key International and Commercial demand down by 15 percent of the response to lowering the thermostat by three degrees from 22 degrees Celsius to 19 degrees Celsius
claims.claim: In Andurand's balance model, a 15% cut in residential/commercial gas via 3 degrees C lower thermostats plus a 5% cut in power demand removes the need for Russian gas.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: if if we don't make steps today to lower demand then we will have some issue um some shortage before the end of the winter
claims.claim: Without early demand cuts Europe faces shortage before the end of winter because storage would run out.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: the LNG Imports we present 71 of the import capacity of Europe
claims.claim: European LNG import terminals were running at about 71% of capacity with floating units arriving, so terminals are not binding; the constraint is global LNG supply.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: Global Supply of LNG is about 550 BCM so that's billion cubic meters and it's growing for the next few years um at around 15 BCM per year for the next two years
claims.claim: Global LNG supply of about 550 bcm grows only 15 bcm per year for two years and then about 60 bcm a year, so Europe would have to take about 40% of additions and live with cooler temperatures for two years.
claims.direction: gas stays tight for two years

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: all the consumers have an incentive in playing game and you know bang bang oil cheaper than what they've done you know in the past
claims.claim: A G7 price cap on Russian oil is enforceable because most buyers gain from cheaper oil, though there will be some cheating.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: lower than current prices obviously and and lower than where China and India are buying it
claims.claim: To work the cap must be set below current market prices and below what China and India now pay, so that Russia still sells but earns less without cutting supply.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: if you have to replace all the oil exports to Europe and move them to India and China you need a lot more ships
claims.claim: Rerouting Russian oil to Asia needs many more ships, many of them Greek, so shipping capacity limits cap enforcement and cheating.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: some processes you need natural gas as a fixed token you cannot change it right but some of them you can
claims.claim: Some industrial uses (chemicals, glass, petrochemicals) need gas as feedstock and cannot switch, but many can use naphtha or oil, so industrial demand destruction is partial; strategic industries need government support.
claims.indicator: industrial gas feedstock vs fuel use

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: over the next two to three years it will be resolved through more LNG
claims.claim: The gas shortage should be resolved within two to three years through more LNG and lower unnecessary consumption.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: there should be a switch to to Really invest massively into nuclear like around Europe
claims.claim: Europe needs massive investment in nuclear for base-load low-carbon capacity, but plants take years to build; French reactors at 40 years need maintenance.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: the warmer temperatures in the summer make it more difficult to cool uh nuclear reactors so that's why some of them have to shut
claims.claim: Hot summers force nuclear reactors cooled by rivers or sea to shut down, reducing power supply in heat waves worldwide.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: we have to make sure that the demand meat Supply as well because if demand is above Supply eventually you have shortages
claims.claim: Subsidies and consumer price caps (UK) leave demand above supply and risk shortages and blackouts; prices must reflect scarcity, and France's regulated prices only rose 4% while UK wholesale pass-through doubled.
claims.testable: partly - demand response to capped vs uncapped prices

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: you can't print energy right you can import some of it but you have limits to how much you want to you can import
claims.claim: Energy cannot be printed and imports are limited to what is available globally, so overbidding for a cargo another country needs raises prices and shifts the bill to taxpayers.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: so I think government should do more um to motivate to encourage I mean first to explain why to go on a public awareness campaign
claims.claim: Governments should run public awareness campaigns to cut demand, because price signals alone will not balance a market where supply is falling.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: we had the largest SBR release ever um you know basically by 160 million barrels
claims.claim: The US led the largest strategic reserve release ever (about 160 million barrels over six months, around 1 mb/d, plus 0.5 mb/d from others), which more than offset a Russian loss of only about 0.5 mb/d.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: the Russian invasion of Ukraine bought a million barrels a day more production more Supply on the market
claims.claim: Net of SPR releases and little Russian loss, the war added about 1 mb/d of supply, helping explain oil falling since summer.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: the fact that Market participants were expecting Russian Supply to go down by roughly 2 million barrels a day and we have not seen that yet
claims.claim: Oil fell since the summer because the expected 2 mb/d Russian supply loss did not appear, SPR supply rose and demand and recession fears grew.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: the EU embargo has not started yet right so we are starting in uh could in early December and then products in early February
claims.claim: The EU embargo on Russian crude starts early December and on products early February, so actual Russian supply loss is still ahead.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: I believe we're gonna lose some Russian Supply I don't know how much but I would say between one and two million barrels a day
claims.claim: Andurand expects to lose 1-2 mb/d of Russian supply, from the embargo, and from Putin's reaction to the price cap.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: the spr release will have to stop I mean already I think the pace of the release is going to slow down now
claims.claim: The SPR release is finite and slowing, so a supply source that depressed prices ends.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: there's probably two million barrels a day of demand that can come back once China you know reopens to the world
claims.claim: Chinese reopening could add about 2 mb/d of oil demand after lockdowns curbed consumption.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: the only negative event is uh is is a global recession
claims.claim: Event risks (Russia, SPR end, China reopening) are mostly positive for oil, and the main negative is a global recession, so medium-term risks are skewed up while the short term is dominated by recession worry.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: look at my supply and demand balance for the next few years to me it looks bullish right
claims.claim: Despite the market trading as if it wants to go lower day to day, the multi-year supply-demand balance says prices must go higher.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: they're at 11 million barrels a day production they've never had they've never you know managed to to have that level of production for more than a month
claims.claim: There is almost no spare capacity; Saudi Arabia is producing 11 mb/d, a level never sustained for more than a month before, and most OPEC members are at maximum.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: instead of going like one to 1.5 million miles a day I think they will grow around half a million dollars a day over the next couple of years
claims.claim: US shale growth should slow from 1-1.5 mb/d a year to about 0.5 mb/d a year, so supply growth is limited.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: it's a mix of you know the low hanging foot having been taken already
claims.claim: Shale response is weak due to depleted best acreage, supply-chain and fracking-equipment constraints and shareholder pressure for restraint.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: the decline rate for Shayla like 80 percent the first year so they need to really keep on drilling
claims.claim: Shale wells decline about 80% in the first year, so producers must keep drilling just to hold output, and cutting drilling quickly reduces production.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: the day where we went down ten dollars a barrel from from like 95 to like from 105 to 95 dollars in less than 24 hours and there was no
claims.claim: Oil futures moved $10 in 24 hours on no news, showing the market had become disconnected from information because of illiquidity.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: it went from 1.4 billion Barrels in 2018 to 300 million today
claims.claim: Non-commercial net longs in oil (CFTC data) fell from 1.4 billion barrels in 2018 to 300 million, so there are far fewer speculative longs.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: if a market is twice as volatile they're gonna have half of the position in barrels than they used to have and so that leads to a bit of a Snowball Effect
claims.claim: Funds scale positions inversely to volatility, so higher volatility cuts positions and liquidity, creating a snowball of more volatility.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: you have some hedging that has to go through which is the main the same type of volume than in the past but in the in the market that is a lot less liquid
claims.claim: Fixed hedging flows in a thinner market move prices much more than before.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: if nobody is willing to come and think it's it's cheap to buy it nobody has any risk appetite anymore then then the price doesn't mean anything
claims.claim: With no risk appetite from buyers, the oil price stops carrying information and can fall far on no news, which also hurts producers' financing.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: we've had like a structural bullish position on energy and that worked well in the first half of the year and then we gave back some gains
claims.claim: Andurand held a structural bullish energy position that worked in H1 2022 and gave back gains in the following months.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: I don't understand really what's going on in the market uh you know I might disagree but I don't understand so I don't want to be too stubborn and and I want to to reduce my positions
claims.claim: When the market moves against a thesis for reasons not understood, cut positions to focus on survival rather than stubbornly defending the view.
claims.testable: partly - rule-based cut after adverse moves testable

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: I think U.S is probably going to be close to half of the the LNG growth
claims.claim: The US should supply about half of global LNG additions over three to four years, so US gas producers with export access benefit.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: there will still be you know a lot of money in moving cargos until the U.S has export capacity which I think is not before you know 2026 or 2027
claims.claim: Until new US export terminals open (2026-27) energy prices stay high and moving cargoes remains highly profitable.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: quite positive for you know all the natural gas producers that can export
claims.claim: Thematic positioning for the European energy redesign: long US gas producers with export capacity.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: just being long uranium is probably a good trade being long the companies that build nuclear reactors
claims.claim: Energy security should boost uranium, nuclear reactor builders, solar and wind as Europe re-architects supply.
claims.indicator: uranium, nuclear builders, solar and wind

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: this energy security issue will only I think should accelerate the transition because when you deal with nuclear wind or power you're you know you're not giving that money to autocratic regimes
claims.claim: Energy security concerns accelerate decarbonization, because renewables and nuclear avoid funding autocratic suppliers; the problem is that decarbonization was not fast enough.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: in the short term to keep the lights on to make sure we don't have you know social and rest we have to accept that mock code is being used
claims.claim: Coal and oil use must rise for two to three years to keep the lights on while low-carbon capacity is built as fast as possible.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: we can deal with 10 or 15 percent less as enough fat in the system someone in consumption but you can't really deal with 50 less
claims.claim: Society can absorb a 10-15% energy cut but not 50% without social unrest and a financial crisis, so the policy target is moderate demand cuts plus new supply.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: early this year I became less bullish on carbon so on carbon prices the euas the carbon Credit in Europe because I think now the mandates will come you know from the top down
claims.claim: Andurand became less bullish on EU carbon allowances because energy security will drive top-down mandates for nuclear and renewables, reducing the role of the carbon price.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: I think it will accelerate it I mean because it's an energy security issue right
claims.claim: Nationalization of utilities (such as Uniper) accelerates the shift to renewables and nuclear because governments act on energy security.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: it's generally generally the countries that have the most issues to start with right so it's more like emerging markets that are an important importers of natural gas
claims.claim: In a bidding war for gas, stress falls on poor importers such as Sri Lanka and Pakistan, which become energy poor, a spillover risk for emerging markets.
claims.direction: avoid or short vulnerable EM importers

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: that will be marginally bullish oil but um it will displace Natural Gas um demand so basically you'll have a bit less demand for natural gas
claims.claim: Gas-to-oil switching in the West is marginally bullish for oil but frees gas cargoes for poorer importers, easing the bidding war.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: I do suspect the the natural gas prices to stay high generally for the next two years
claims.claim: Natural gas prices should stay high for the next two years, with the first step down if the winter is managed with little Russian gas.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: the first step down will be if we can manage this winter properly
claims.claim: Managing winter with low Russian gas removes the psychological fear premium and gives a large price impact lower.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: there's two conflicting forces one is how much oil we will lose from Russia
claims.claim: Key oil uncertainties are the amount of Russian supply lost after the price cap and the state of the global economy.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: much higher interest rates and still high energy Pisces and the worries about the war and and all that you know makes people want to spend less
claims.claim: Sharp central-bank rate hikes plus high energy prices weaken consumer and business demand, creating a demand-side risk to oil prices.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: more aggressive Russia becomes the easier it is to accept some pain on our side
claims.claim: Europe's willingness to bear pain rises with Russian aggression because of a war mindset, so energy demand cuts are politically durable.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: eventually with time possession will go down anyway due to the lack of
claims.claim: Russian production will decline with time because sanctions block equipment, expertise and investment, plus mobilization effects.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: moving the the thermostat down by one degree has an impact of 10 BCM uh for the for Europe so that's uh about five percent or so
claims.claim: The IEA estimates each degree lower thermostat saves about 10 bcm (about 5%) of European gas, so 3 degrees is about 15%.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: consumption as a percentage of income has been going down in general so energy has been relatively abundant and and cheap
claims.claim: Over almost 30 years energy took a falling share of income, so households heated homes more warmly, meaning there is room to cut without much hardship.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: have to switch into a war Paradigm and once we understand that uh I don't think the steps we have to make are are too difficult
claims.claim: The energy shock requires moving from a mindset of abundance to a war paradigm; once governments accept planning for no Russian gas, the demand-side steps needed are modest and manageable.
claims.conditions: Depends on political acceptance of the new regime.
claims.testable: no - qualitative judgement on policy reaction

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: Russia would not get 100 billion dollars of European money as a result
claims.claim: If Europe closes its gas balance through demand cuts and LNG, Russia loses about $100 billion of European gas revenue, so demand reduction is also a sanctions tool.
claims.indicator: Russian gas export revenue from Europe (about $100 billion)
claims.conditions: Requires the demand cuts of about 15% in heating and 5% in power.
claims.testable: partly - revenue loss is computable from volumes and prices

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: we were living with 15 to 16 degrees in the 70s uh you know during the the energy crisis of the 70s
claims.claim: Historical analogues make a 3 degree thermostat cut credible: indoor temperatures of 19 degrees match the mid-1990s average in Europe and the UK, and in the 1970s energy crisis homes were kept at 15 to 16 degrees.
claims.direction: lower gas demand is achievable without hardship
claims.testable: partly - based on historical household temperature surveys

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: it looks like um you know the work mainly at those power prices the work will be done for some of that capacity to come back online
claims.claim: Very high power prices give operators a strong incentive to finish maintenance on the ageing French nuclear fleet, so part of the offline capacity should return, easing the power and gas squeeze.
claims.conditions: Plants near their 40-year design life need repairs, so recovery is partial.
claims.testable: partly - availability versus power price could be tracked

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: the volumes are much lower than in the past the open interest has gone down a lot also in terms of uh positions
claims.claim: Oil futures volume and open interest have fallen sharply, so the market is thinner and the same fixed flows move prices more.
claims.indicator: oil futures volume and open interest
claims.direction: larger price swings per unit of flow
claims.testable: yes - exchange volume and open interest series

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: generally it's been down more easily than ever I would say
claims.claim: In the illiquid 2022 oil market, large no-news price moves have been skewed to the downside, because buyers have no risk appetite and a single seller or bidder can push the price down.
claims.indicator: oil price asymmetry in thin markets
claims.direction: price drops on no news more than rises
claims.conditions: Thin liquidity and low speculative length.
claims.testable: partly - skewness of daily moves versus liquidity could be tested

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: generally gas to all these are cheapest actually because now oil is even cheaper than coal
claims.claim: Gas-to-oil switching is the cheapest substitution route because oil is now even cheaper than coal per unit of energy, so switching away from gas supports oil demand rather than coal.
claims.indicator: relative price of gas, oil and coal per unit energy
claims.direction: oil demand marginally up, gas demand down
claims.conditions: Valid while the oil price is below coal on an energy-equivalent basis.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: not only we can avoid shortages but also it will bring prices down significantly
claims.claim: Public awareness campaigns that cut non-essential demand do two things: avoid physical shortages and bring gas prices down significantly, which helps the global economy.
claims.indicator: gas price response to demand reduction
claims.conditions: Needs coordinated action in the importing countries.
claims.testable: partly - price elasticity of the marginal LNG cargo could be estimated

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: that's a study that was made in 2014 basically to look at the impact of winter indoor indoor domestic temperatures on on Health in general
claims.claim: Andurand sizes the thermostat saving from published data: the IEA's estimate of about 10 bcm (5%) per degree and a 2014 study of indoor winter temperatures for the historical baseline.
claims.indicator: IEA thermostat sensitivity, 2014 indoor temperature study
claims.conditions: Linear scaling assumed for three degrees.
claims.testable: partly - the sources are cited but the linear assumption is untested
